Guide

How to book meetings before a trade show or conference

By Or Alperovitz, founder of A8Z · Updated November 1, 2026

Short answer: Start 6-8 weeks before the event. Spend 1-2 weeks building a list of attendees and target accounts that match your ICP. Then run 4-6 weeks of personalized email and LinkedIn outreach that names the event, gives a specific reason to meet, and offers a short meeting at a concrete place and time. Confirm every meeting with a calendar invite, send reminders during event week, and follow up with everyone after the show.

Why pre-booking matters

A conference trip for a small vendor team costs real money: passes, flights, hotels, and often a booth. Most small teams still plan to "work the floor" and hope for walk-ups. At big shows like RSAC or KubeCon, hundreds of vendors compete for the same buyers, and the buyers who matter arrive with calendars that are already full.

The teams that come back with pipeline booked their meetings before they got on the plane.

The timeline

WhenWhat to do
8 weeks outSet goals (how many meetings, with whom), define ICP and personas, decide where meetings will happen.
6-8 weeks outBuild the target list: attendees, exhibitors, speakers, side-event hosts, and your own target accounts that are attending.
4-6 weeks outLaunch outreach: email and LinkedIn, 3-4 touches over 2-3 weeks.
1-2 weeks outLast-call message to non-responders, confirm booked meetings, share a meeting schedule with your team.
Event weekReminders the day before, handle reschedules, log notes after each meeting.
1-10 days afterFollow up with everyone you met, and with people who wanted to meet but couldn't.

Step 1: Decide who you actually want to meet

Don't treat the attendee or exhibitor list as your lead list. Filter it to the companies and roles that match your ICP. For most B2B tech vendors that means a few hundred people at most, not thousands. Separate them into tiers: target accounts you're already pursuing, new ICP accounts, and partners.

Step 2: Find out who's going

  • Exhibitor and sponsor lists on the event website. Exhibitors send their sales, marketing and leadership teams.
  • Speaker lists and agendas. Speakers are confirmed attendees and often senior.
  • LinkedIn posts. Search for people posting "heading to", "see you at" or the event hashtag in the weeks before.
  • Side events. Event aggregators and Luma pages list the dinners, parties and meetups around big conferences, with hosts and sometimes guests.
  • Your own CRM. Ask open opportunities and customers if they're attending.

Step 3: Write outreach that earns a meeting

Three rules: mention the event in the first line, give one specific reason the meeting is worth their time, and make saying yes easy with a concrete place and two time options.

Example first email:

Hi Dana, noticed Acme is at KubeCon in Barcelona. Teams running multi-cluster setups like yours usually lose hours every week to [specific problem]. We're showing how [peer company type] cut that by [result] in 20 minutes at booth S42. Tuesday 11:00 or Wednesday 14:30?

Follow with a LinkedIn connection a few days later, then a short bump that adds one new piece of value, and a final "last call" message the week before the event.

Step 4: Pick meeting places that work

Your booth is one option, not the only one. Hotel lobbies, cafes near the venue, side events and the prospect's own booth all work, and they're the only options if you don't have a booth. Keep meetings to 20-30 minutes and leave buffers: the expo floor is slow to cross.

Step 5: Protect the meetings during the show

Send a reminder the day before with the exact location. Expect some reschedules and handle them fast. Have one person own the shared meeting calendar so nobody double-books.

Step 6: Follow up after the event

Send follow-ups within a few days while the conversation is fresh. Also reach the people who wanted to meet but couldn't: "Missed you at RSAC, want to do the 20 minutes on Zoom instead?" often converts better than the original outreach.

Common mistakes

  • Starting outreach the week before the event, when calendars are already full.
  • Emailing the whole attendee list with the same template.
  • "Stop by our booth" as the only call to action, with no time and no reason.
  • No follow-up after the show.
